title: Blog 1
content:
DOES SQS FIFO REALLY GUARANTEE “EXACTLY-ONCE PROCESSING”? An interesting scenario when studying asynchronous systems on AWS: an application receives the event “Order #1042 has been created”. AWS Lambda processes the message from Amazon SQS FIFO and writes to DynamoDB successfully, but the function times out just before it removes the message from SQS. The same message is then received again. If we already use a FIFO queue, why can reprocessing still happen? This post clarifies the difference between duplicate-send prevention, order preservation, and preventing duplicate business effects, based on the AWS Documentation.
Key points to remember:
Standard Queue offers very high throughput and at-least-once delivery, but messages may be received more than once or out of order. FIFO Queue supports ordering within each MessageGroupId and message deduplication; different groups can be processed in parallel.
SQS FIFO’s “exactly-once” is duplicate-send prevention at the messaging layer. It does not mean the whole business logic in Lambda runs exactly once.
Deduplication has only a 5-minute window: if a producer resends the same MessageDeduplicationId within 5 minutes, SQS does not add another copy to the queue. If it is resent after that, the message may be treated as new.
With content-based deduplication enabled, SQS generates the deduplication ID from the SHA-256 of the message body, not including message attributes. So changing attributes does not make a different message for deduplication purposes.
Lambda + SQS can still process duplicates: event source mappings have at-least-once semantics. If processing fails or times out, the message reappears after the visibility timeout and is received again, even though the data was already written successfully.
Idempotency means performing the same request multiple times still gives the same business result as performing it once. For example, use DynamoDB PutItem with ConditionExpression: attribute\_not\_exists(eventId) so a later attempt does not overwrite the existing item.
A PutItem condition only prevents duplicate writes for that item; it does not create end-to-end exactly-once. If a workflow also sends emails, calls a payment API, or updates multiple systems, you need additional transactions/outbox, a processing state, or downstream API idempotency.
Retry and partial batch response: by default, if one message in a batch fails, the whole batch may be retried. Enable ReportBatchItemFailures to report only the failed messages. For FIFO, stop after the first failure and report all unprocessed messages as well, so ordering is not broken.
Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ): configure a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount to move repeatedly failing messages to a DLQ; a FIFO source queue must use a FIFO DLQ. A DLQ helps isolate and investigate failures, but it can break strict business ordering when reprocessing and does not guarantee messages will eventually succeed on their own.
4 questions when designing an async system:
Must events be processed in order within each group? If so, MessageGroupId must represent the right business flow, for example orderId. If a message reappears after 5 minutes or Lambda retries, is it safe to run the logic again? Do the visibility timeout, batch failure handling, and retry policy fit the real processing time? If a message fails permanently, how will the operations team detect it, handle it, and redrive the DLQ? Conclusion: “exactly-once delivery/deduplication” at the messaging layer is different from “exactly-once business effect” at the application layer. A reliable workflow needs FIFO semantics, visibility timeout, retry/DLQ, idempotency, and side-effect control designed together.

title: 5.1 · Problem and architecture
content:
An employee forwards a suspicious email while a colleague submits a screenshot of the same campaign. SecOps needs to preserve both originals, establish who can read each report and record the reason for a decision. This lab builds that process in US East (N. Virginia).
Open the full-resolution diagram · draw.io
How to read the diagram The browser loads React through CloudFront. Cognito issues a JWT. The HTTP API validates it for the Reporter and Admin APIs. The APIs use DynamoDB to check ownership, read incidents and record decisions. A browser uploads an image or EML directly to S3 using a presigned POST returned by the Reporter API. For pasted text or a demo fixture the Reporter API writes/copies the object. All three web paths produce uploads/{uuid}/raw. An S3 ObjectCreated notification calls Ingest. SES uses a separate receipt rule: store the original MIME in inbound/, then invoke Ingest with receipt verdicts. Ingest validates, computes SHA-256 and saves the raw object in the evidence bucket with versioning, SSE-KMS and seven-day Governance retention. After the save it starts the execution named for the incident, passing evidence references including raw_s3_key, raw_s3_version_id when available, and evidence_sha256. The sanitized bucket holds a separate redacted analysis copy. The SQS dead-letter queue receives failed async Ingest deliveries. Extract & Redact reads the evidence, runs Vietnamese/English Tesseract for images, and masks detectable PII. Insufficient usable text and QR evidence leads to NEEDS_MORE_INFO. Triage scores rules and checks indicators. Synthesize retrieves playbook passages and requests a Bedrock summary when configured. A deterministic fallback stays visible when synthesis fails. A high/critical report without a valid action goes to NEEDS_REVIEW with an SNS notice. A lower-risk report without a proposal ends at NO_ACTION. With a valid proposal, PrepareApproval persists the token and PENDING_APPROVAL before notifying SecOps. The Standard workflow holds the wait. The Lambda invocation returns. An admin reads the proposal and submits a decision. Admin API checks state and role, then calls SendTaskSuccess with the decision. Rejection ends at REJECTED. Expiry follows the timeout path to ESCALATED_TIMEOUT. An approval in the observed DRY_RUN mode records the simulated result and audit trail. Any blocklist entry is internal. External mail/firewall enforcement is outside this deployment. Two boundaries to point out. PhishGuardEdge protects traffic through CloudFront. The signed upload goes directly to S3. Lambda uses AWS-managed networking in this SAM template. The region and the service groups indicate placement and responsibility. QR extraction reads a URL locally, strips query and fragment for display, and supplies an indicator to Triage. The approval callback belongs to the Step Functions task that invokes PrepareApproval.

title: Blog 2
content:
HOW CAN A SMALL IAM PERMISSION CAUSE A BIG RISK? AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management) lets administrators control user access to AWS services and resources. However, granting overly broad permissions, especially AdministratorAccess, can create serious security vulnerabilities if the account’s credentials are leaked or the account is compromised. This post analyzes the risks when an IAM account with full administrative access to AWS is breached, and the solutions to reduce them.
Key points to remember:
AdministratorAccess is an AWS Managed Policy that allows almost every administrative action in an AWS account, so if it is compromised, an attacker can affect the entire system. Amazon S3: an attacker can download or delete data, or change bucket access permissions → leakage of customer information and internal data. Amazon EC2: an attacker can launch unauthorized instances for cryptocurrency mining (Cryptojacking) or delete running servers → higher costs and service disruption. Amazon RDS: an attacker can delete databases, delete snapshots, or change security settings → data loss and impact on applications. AWS IAM: an attacker can create new users/roles, attach administrator policies, and create Access Keys to maintain access → incident response becomes more complicated. AWS CloudTrail: an attacker can stop or change logging configuration → loss of monitoring and investigation capability if logs are not protected independently. Least Privilege: grant only the permissions that are truly needed, and avoid AdministratorAccess when administration is not required. MFA: enable multi-factor authentication for important accounts to protect them when passwords are leaked. IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials: prefer temporary credentials over storing long-term Access Keys in applications. Permission Boundaries: set the maximum permissions that an IAM User or Role can receive. CloudTrail Monitoring: monitor API activity, especially changes related to IAM and security configuration. Regular Access Review: regularly review and revoke permissions that are no longer needed, and detect overly broad policies. This post is especially useful for anyone operating systems on AWS who wants to tighten permission management, because a small but overly broad IAM permission can lead to major consequences.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS ACCESS KEY LEAKED ON GITHUB: AWS AUTOMATICALLY QUARANTINED IT, SO WHAT ELSE DO WE NEED TO DO? When I first read about AWS Access Key exposure incidents, I assumed AWS already had automatic detection and handling, so the risk wasn’t too worrying. After looking into it more closely, I realized that was only partly true: AWS can help detect and limit the damage, but that doesn’t mean our account is safe. This post explains what AWS actually does when a key is exposed, the steps we still need to take, and how to prevent it.
Key points to remember:
AWS can detect credentials that are publicly exposed on sources such as GitHub. When it does, it may apply a quarantine policy (AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 or V4) to the related IAM identity and send a notification through AWS Health or a Support Case. In one Unit 42 experiment, AWS attached the V3 policy about 10 seconds after the key was made public. This is the result of a specific test, not a guaranteed response time in every case. A quarantine policy does not disable the access key. It only adds Deny permissions for certain specific actions, while other actions still depend on the identity’s other IAM permissions. Step 1 – Isolate the credential: identify the IAM user that owns the key, assess its permission scope, and set the key to Inactive. Avoid deleting it right away so it remains available for cross-checking. Step 2 – Restore legitimate access: identify the workloads using the old key, update them with valid credentials, and consider moving to IAM Roles that use temporary credentials. Step 3 – Investigate with CloudTrail: review which APIs were called, when, from which IP, in which Region, and any unusual IAM changes. Use a separate admin principal to investigate. Event History mainly contains management events, while data events (such as S3 object access) must have been configured for logging beforehand. Step 4 – Check for signs of compromise across the whole account: new or unexpectedly changed IAM users/roles/policies, unfamiliar EC2/Lambda resources, unauthorized S3 access, rarely used Regions, and abnormal Billing charges. Step 5 – Complete remediation: don’t remove the quarantine policy just because the application works again; follow the guidance in the AWS Support Case. Prevention: use IAM Roles for workloads, IAM Identity Center/Federation for users, GitHub Actions OIDC instead of long-term access keys, enable GitHub Secret Scanning & Push Protection, and use pre-commit hooks such as git-secrets. Removing a secret from a file or commit does not make the credential safe. Once exposed publicly, treat it as possibly copied and follow the incident response process. My takeaway: no automatic mechanism can replace proper management of identities, permissions, and credentials. In the Cloud, security isn’t only about preventing unauthorized access, but also knowing how to detect, investigate, isolate, and recover when an incident happens.
How do you manage AWS credentials for personal or team projects? Especially with GitHub Actions, do you use OIDC or still store access keys in GitHub Secrets? I’d love to hear real-world experience.

title: Event 2
content:
Event Report: “AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi 2026” General Information Event: AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi 2026 Time: 09:00 – 17:00, September 29, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Participant Why I Attended and What I Expected Understand why cloud, Generative AI, and Agentic AI are moving out of the lab and into real enterprise operations. Catch up on how to build cloud-native applications, infrastructure, data platforms, workload identity, and AI governance. See how Vietnamese enterprises and AWS modernize systems at scale. Learn how security, governance, observability, and human oversight must grow as AI becomes more autonomous. Connect the event’s content to my own direction in cybersecurity and cloud security. Guests and Speakers Dr. Werner Vogels – CTO, Amazon.com, keynote speaker Eric Yeo – Country General Manager for Malaysia, Vietnam & Indochina, AWS Mai Le – Director of Product Management, Katalon Dr. Jens Lottner – Chief Executive Officer, Techcombank Experts, architects, and technology leaders from AWS, Katalon, Techcombank, TCBS, Techcom Life, VPBank, and other organizations Key Highlights From Cloud-Native Architecture to Agentic AI The trend goes beyond “moving servers to the cloud” toward building flexible, highly automated systems based on containers, Kubernetes, serverless, event-driven architecture, and managed services. Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms provide ready-made “Golden Paths”, so developers wait less on manual ticket approvals to get infrastructure. The tools mentioned include Amazon EKS, Crossplane, Terragrunt, Backstage, FluxCD, and GitOps, which make deployments consistent, repeatable, and easy to audit. Taking AI Agents from Prototype to Production Building a working agent is easy; keeping it safe in operation is hard. Four pillars must be met:
Operational excellence: reliability, error handling, latency, and continuous monitoring. Data governance: who owns the data, how fresh it is, its quality, and who can access it. Security and trust: control over identity, allowed tools, permissions, and sensitive information. Human oversight: actions with high impact or that cannot be undone must have a responsible person. Sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Bedrock AgentCore, Strands Agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP), and the ReAct model showed how an agent reasons, looks up information, calls tools, retains context, and acts within a defined permission scope.
Identity, Least Privilege, and AI Security Instead of only removing long-lived access keys, the new direction is to give workloads an identity that can be verified across multiple trust boundaries. Key mechanisms include AWS IAM, AWS STS (short-lived credentials), trust policies, session policies, session tags, source identity, and ABAC, applied to EC2, ECS/Fargate, Lambda, EKS, CI/CD, multi-account systems, and AI agents. AI Governance and Data Security Enterprise AI is not just about choosing a model; it is a data and governance problem: accuracy, freshness, provenance, ownership, access control, evidence behind answers, and decision traceability. The security chain is summarized as: Identity → Data → Model → Tools → Agent → Action → Audit. Security Observability for AI Applications The traditional four golden signals (latency, errors, traffic, saturation) need to be extended with:
Cost: token consumption and unusual spikes. Safety: personal data exposure, prompt injection, and tools used for the wrong purpose. Quality: hallucinations and inaccurate answers. Monitoring data should be combined from infrastructure, security events, data access, and agent behavior.
AI-Assisted Software Development, Done Securely Kiro and AI-DLC bring AI into the entire development lifecycle: planning, design, coding, testing, documentation, deployment, technical debt handling, and modernization. TCBS reported about a 26% reduction in development time. The conditions are verification, security review, governance, human approval, and DevSecOps integration. Cloud Modernization and Enterprise Security Cases from Techcombank, Techcom Life, TCBS, VPBank, and Katalon centered on application and database modernization, containerization, data platform consolidation, infrastructure automation, observability, compliance, and resilience. For data-residency requirements, AWS introduced the Local Zone in Hanoi and second-generation AWS Outposts. The common challenge is balancing security, compliance, reliability, performance, cost, and business agility. Lessons Learned Security Mindset Identity is a security boundary. Every workload, pipeline, service, and AI agent should have its own identity with short-lived credentials and least-privilege access. Protect the whole AI chain from identity to audit, and let humans decide at high-risk steps. Extend monitoring to AI behavior, data access, safety, quality, and cost. Architecture and Engineering Prefer reproducible and traceable infrastructure (managed services, containers, serverless, IaC, GitOps) over logging in via SSH to make manual fixes. Combine IAM, STS, ABAC, and multi-account access with trustworthy data sources. AI and Cybersecurity Agents must be evaluated on whether they work with the right identity, permissions, data, and evidence, because AI opens new attack surfaces such as prompt injection, data leakage, excessive permissions, unauthorized actions, hallucination, and hard-to-control costs. Cloud Security, DevSecOps, AI Security, and Security Operations are increasingly intertwined. How I Plan to Apply This Practice least-privilege IAM with short-lived credentials: build a small lab with a role, trust policy, and session tags, then check the traces in the audit logs. Expand monitoring: collect infrastructure logs, identity events, application telemetry, and AI agent activity; explore bringing Wazuh and SIEM into cloud and AI security. Apply GitOps and IaC to infrastructure changes, and set boundaries for permissions, data, logging, and approvals when experimenting with AI agents. Use AI tools to speed up work while keeping security review and human approval, and connect network/endpoint security knowledge with cloud-native security. Personal Reflection The event gave me a broad view of system modernization, agentic AI, and security at enterprise scale.
Hearing AWS leaders and enterprises share showed me that technology always has to go hand in hand with governance, operations, security, and organizational change. Real-world examples tied cloud and AI knowledge to compliance requirements and true production scale. Automation without governance can raise risk as fast as it raises productivity. The more autonomous a system is, the tighter identity and permission control must be. Security professionals must not only detect attacks but also know how to protect, monitor, and govern AI systems themselves. Check-in Photos

title: 2. Project proposal
content:
PhishGuard AI · Omnichannel phishing triage with human approval
Proposed pilot: an internal security operations team and employees reporting suspicious messages. Deployment region: US East (N. Virginia). The demo runs containment in DRY_RUN.
The operational problem An employee forwards a suspicious message to a general mailbox. A second employee reports an image of the same campaign. The analyst needs to identify each reporter, preserve precisely what each person submitted, explain a recommendation and find the decision later. Copying text into a chatbot helps with interpretation. Someone still has to connect the evidence, access controls, reviewer and outcome.
What the pilot delivers A Cognito-authenticated portal accepts pasted text, screenshots and EML files. An SES receiving rule accepts forwarded email from verified reporters. Ingest gives each report an incident ID and preserves a version of the original. Analysts use a redacted copy for routine work. A separate, audited request gives a privileged analyst short-lived access to the original.
The policy engine computes the score from indicators and named rules. Bedrock can retrieve playbooks and explain the result. If generation fails, the analyst still sees the rule result and the fallback reason. Where an action is proposed, Step Functions records a deadline, notifies SecOps and resumes only on a valid decision or a timeout. Approval records retain the human decision. A simulated block, a confirmed entry in the internal list and enforcement by an external product have different operational effects. External enforcement is outside the pilot.
Deliverables and acceptance Milestone Deliverable How to accept it Intake and preservation Portal, SES and separate evidence stores Submit a UTF-8 message and an image, then trace an incident to its S3 version. Repeating the same reporter request returns its incident. Analysis OCR, PII masking, policy evaluation and grounded summary Inspect the extracted Vietnamese text, triggered rules and evidence. Low-quality input asks for more information. Record the actual synthesis status. Approval Admin decision, callback and audit log An approved demo produces an audit record. An unanswered request expires. A late decision returns HTTP 409. Operations and handover Role-specific reads, alarms, workshop and cost model A second reporter cannot read the first reporter’s incident. Demonstrate alarm targets, a reproducible deployment and the assumptions behind cost. Boundaries and risks Object Lock Governance protects a raw version for seven days subject to authorized bypass. OCR may miss accents and masking can leave names or addresses. Forwarded headers describe the original message as supplied by the employee. SES authentication proves facts about the outer delivery. Analysts must interpret those separately. False-positive and false-negative rates on unseen real-world messages still require a labelled evaluation set.
Deployed scope. The CloudFront distribution has the PhishGuardEdge web ACL. Raw uploads go directly to S3. Image extraction supports Vietnamese/English OCR and URL QR codes. Five source playbooks support retrieval. Triage proposes eligible actions and Bedrock explains them.
Costs and pilot decision For a 30-day month with 300 reports, 90 images and 60 inbound emails, the model estimates USD 9.37, including the permanent WAF rules and one hosted zone. The Cost Explorer report for 1–23 November 2026 rounds to USD 0.00 within its export scope. Before extending the pilot, compare time to triage, false alerts, missed cases and manual review against the current mailbox process using an independently labelled set.
Architecture walkthrough · Cost model and billing evidence

title: Blogs Posted
content:
This section will list and introduce the blogs you have posted to AWS Study Group. For example:
Blog 1 - DOES SQS FIFO REALLY GUARANTEE “EXACTLY-ONCE PROCESSING” AWS Lambda processes the message from Amazon SQS FIFO and writes to DynamoDB successfully, but the function times out just before it removes the message from SQS. The same message is then received again. If we already use a FIFO queue, why can reprocessing still happen? This post clarifies the difference between duplicate-send prevention, order preservation, and preventing duplicate business effects, based on the AWS Documentation.
Blog 2 - HOW CAN A SMALL IAM PERMISSION CAUSE A BIG RISK AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management) lets administrators control user access to AWS services and resources. However, granting overly broad permissions, especially AdministratorAccess, can create serious security vulnerabilities if the account’s credentials are leaked or the account is compromised. This post analyzes the risks when an IAM account with full administrative access to AWS is breached, and the solutions to reduce them.
Blog 3 - AWS ACCESS KEY LEAKED ON GITHUB: AWS AUTOMATICALLY QUARANTINED IT, SO WHAT ELSE DO WE NEED TO DO When I first read about AWS Access Key exposure incidents, I assumed AWS already had automatic detection and handling, so the risk wasn’t too worrying. After looking into it more closely, I realized that was only partly true: AWS can help detect and limit the damage, but that doesn’t mean our account is safe. This post explains what AWS actually does when a key is exposed, the steps we still need to take, and how to prevent it.

title: 5.3.3 · Protect CloudFront with WAF
content:
Associate the portal distribution with its web ACL. Two harmless GETs to the same page isolate the temporary header rule. PNG and EML file bytes go directly from the browser to S3 with a presigned POST.
$awsOpts = @('--profile', $pgProfile, '--region', $pgRegion, '--no-cli-pager') function Set-PgWaf([string]$mode, [string]$probe) { aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name phishguard-edge-waf --template-file .\infra\phishguard-waf.yaml --parameter-overrides "ProtectionMode=$mode" "ProbeMode=$probe" RequestsPerMinute=120 --no-fail-on-empty-changeset @awsOpts if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Check CloudFormation stack events.' } } Set-PgWaf COUNT COUNT aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name phishguard-edge-waf --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='WebACLArn'].OutputValue | [0]" --output text @awsOpts $pgDist Run the block above from the lab directory after portal setup. In WAF & Shield → Protection packs (web ACLs) select CloudFront (Global), open PhishGuardEdge → Manage resources → Add global resources, and select the distribution recorded during portal setup. Check the association and allow time for propagation. In COUNT COUNT, run the two GETs below. Both should return 200. In N. Virginia open CloudWatch → Metrics → All metrics → AWS/WAFV2. Select Rule PhishGuardProbe, WebACL PhishGuardEdge, CountedRequests, statistic Sum and period 1 minute. One matching request gives a sum of one in its observation minute. curl.exe -s -o NUL -w "GET: %{http_code}\n" "$pgSite/" curl.exe -s -o NUL -w "Probe: %{http_code}\n" -H "x-phishguard-workshop: verify-edge" "$pgSite/" Run Set-PgWaf COUNT BLOCK, wait for propagation and repeat the GETs. Expect 200 for the ordinary request and 403 for the marked one. Match the time with BlockedRequests for the probe. With COUNT BLOCK, sign in as a reporter. Submit text (202), upload an actual PNG file (presign 201 and S3 POST 204), submit an EML fixture, open its incident, then check the admin dashboard. Inspect the metric name configured for CommonRules. Record missing datapoints as such. Investigate any legitimate match at subrule level before enforcement. After representative transactions pass, run Set-PgWaf ENFORCE OFF. The managed group uses its subrule actions. The configured rate is 120 per IP in a 60-second evaluation window on the two POST routes for reports and presigning. Repeat the business checks and both GETs. Both GETs should now return 200. If WAF disrupts a legitimate operation, use Set-PgWaf COUNT OFF while investigating the matching rule. The demo returned 200/403 with the probe in Block and 200/200 once the probe was off. The graph records a header-rule match. The submission rate threshold was not measured in this test. AWS WAF testing guide

Use the same evidence to examine the design against AWS Well-Architected.
Criterion Decision in PhishGuard Verification and limits Architecture and deployment (0.5) CloudFront has a web ACL. Web and SES submissions converge at Ingest. Raw evidence is saved before the workflow starts. Step Functions owns the approval callback. Compare the behaviors, receipt rule, SAM template and one execution with the arrows in 5.1. Lambda uses AWS-managed networking. The template defines no application subnet. Operational Excellence (0.5) Review change sets before updates. Two alarms notify the SecOps topic about failed executions and Ingest DLQ depth. In 5.5.1 inspect alarm state, actions and topic ARN. Trace a notification timestamp to its execution or Ingest log. Raw evidence has a separate SSE-KMS bucket with versioning and seven-day Governance retention. Approval goes through Admin API. Run H02 and H15 with two reporters and an auditor. Compare ordinary and marked GETs in the WAF test. Direct S3 POSTs are governed by the signed policy and Ingest validation. Restrict Governance bypass privileges. Reliability (0.5) Ingest uses request identity for retries and routes exhausted asynchronous invocations to a DLQ. The workflow handles approval expiry and synthesis can fall back. Exercise H01/H04 and H13/H14 on the demo. For a DLQ message check the cause, incident and raw version before reprocessing. This deployment is single-region. Recovery time and recovery point for a regional outage have not been measured. Performance Efficiency (0.5) Direct upload keeps file bytes out of the HTTP API. Image extraction uses 512 MiB x86_64 Lambda with OCR and QR support. The preparation Lambda returns while the workflow waits for the reviewer. Compare p50/p95 Duration, Billed Duration and Max Memory Used for image and text cohorts with known sizes. Inspect Throttles and measure human approval latency separately. Benchmarks remain open. Cost Optimization (0.5) The model separates report counts, image processing, AI calls and fixed service costs. WAF is the largest line at 300 reports per month. Recalculate the CSV in 5.7, change one assumption and compare with billing for the matching period. Identify shared fees such as the hosted zone and charges that outlive the lab. Sustainability (recorded, 0 points) Event-driven processing and an intake lifecycle limit time and storage spent on temporary work. Check lifecycle rules and older versions after the exercise. Retain evidence through its promised retention period. Workload emissions have not been measured. Responding to an alarm If the DLQ depth alarm fires, record the timestamp and request ID. Find the asynchronous Ingest invocation in CloudWatch Logs. Check access to the source object and required write permissions. Look up the incident, evidence version and execution before retrying a lab event. After recovery, verify the expected number of incidents and executions, confirm that the raw version remains accessible and retain the log explaining the initial failure.
